summary:
Pulsar is an interactive health-monitoring platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, designed to help astronauts monitor and manage their health during space missions.

Our software combines a personalized 3D human avatar with health monitoring, allowing astronauts to visualize their organs, muscles, bones, and cardiovascular system. Using a webcam, Pulsar can measure heart rate and respiratory activity, conduct guided health assessments, and provide personalized recommendations and alerts.

The platform adapts to four space environments: the International Space Station, the Moon, transit to Mars, and the Martian surface. It simulates mission-specific physiological risks, including radiation exposure, muscle and bone loss, and fluid redistribution. Additional features include an augmented-reality helmet interface, eye-tracking controls, guided exercises, and simulated health reporting to Earth.

Our goal is to make astronaut healthcare more accessible, preventive, and autonomous, particularly during long-duration missions where communication delays and limited medical resources make immediate assistance difficult.

Pulsar brings together health monitoring, immersive visualization, and actionable guidance in a single, intuitive platform.
details:
Pulsar is a health monitor for astronauts that runs in a web browser. You open it and see your own body in 3D, inside the place you are living: the space station, the Orion ship on the way to Mars, a base on the Moon or on Mars. Markers on the body stay white when things are fine and turn amber or red when something needs attention. A list on the side tells you what to do today, most urgent first.

Click a part of the body and the camera flies to it. A card shows the value, its trend over 30 days, what to do about it, and the exam NASA runs in flight for the same question. You can peel the body layer by layer, from the EVA suit down to the skin, the vessels, the organs and the skeleton.

Every day comes with a check-up built from your signals: exams that are due, NASA's tasks for that flight day, self-tests and follow-ups. Tick a task and the marker goes back to white. The self-tests use the webcam or the keyboard and measure you, the person at the computer: reaction time, thinking, vision, hearing, balance, sit-to-stand, hand dexterity, pulse recovery, resting pulse and breathing, and exercise reps counted by the camera. Each one is modelled on a NASA test and compared with your own first three runs.

A simulation plays one day of each mission in about three minutes. A CO2 scrubber fails on the station, a solar storm sends the crew to the shelter on the way to Mars, a dust storm cuts a drive short on Mars. In the AR view you see your vitals along the rim of a helmet visor, and you can press its buttons with your eyes using the webcam. At the end of the day, Send to Earth packs the report, encrypts it and sends it over a link with the real delay of the destination, up to 20 minutes from Mars.

Why we built it this way: on a trip to Mars, the crew can't call a doctor and wait for an answer. They need a tool that tells them, in plain words, what is wrong and what to do now. The doctors on Earth still get a full report, just later. Our goal was a tool you understand in seconds, even tired, with no medical training.

What we considered: privacy came first. There is no server. Everything stays in the browser, and the camera only runs during a test and keeps no images. We tied every rule to a published source, mostly NASA's medical requirements and standards, and we wrote down which limits are NASA's and which are ours. The crew's health records are made up for the demo, and Pulsar is not a medical device.

Tools: TypeScript, React 19, Three.js, Vite, Tailwind CSS and Google MediaPipe for face, hand and body tracking. Webcam pulse uses our own versions of the POS and CHROM methods. Anatomy comes from BodyParts3D and the HuBMAP Human Reference Atlas, the bodies from MakeHuman, and the suits from NASA 3D models. Hosted on Vercel. Code, docs, research and credits: https://github.com/4woken/Health-Monitoring-Software

Team: Lucas Baurianne (team owner), Enzo Baurianne, Nassim Arifette and Youssef Mir, from France.
